item.title: Tucker Carlson unveils 10-point manifesto amid third-party speculation
item.description:
Tucker Carlson used a highly promoted livestream Wednesday to unveil a 10-point vision for America — defining the worldview of a breakaway MAGA faction increasingly at odds with President Trump.

Why it matters: After vowing last month to "help build a third party," Carlson fueled further speculation this weekend by hosting MAGA dissidents at his home in Maine, where they urged him to run for president in 2028.

  • The former Fox News host stopped short of a formal launch, instead presenting the manifesto as the foundation for "whatever comes next" — a new political order he said could "find all kinds of expressions."

Zoom in: Carlson said any successor to America's faltering political system should begin with a shared understanding of what the country "should be," which he distilled into 10 points.

  1. Fair: The same rules should apply to presidents, federal agents and elites such as Jeffrey Epstein, whose impunity Carlson cast as emblematic of an "Epstein class" enriching itself through a corrupt system.
  2. Sovereign: Carlson claimed Israel pushed the U.S. into the Iran war through "bribery or threat or both," while describing foreign lobbying, corporate control of government and high-interest debt as forms of "slavery."
  3. Productive: America should rebuild farming, manufacturing and craftsmanship while rejecting an economy dominated by finance, real estate speculation, surveillance systems and weapons.
  4. Beautiful: Carlson alleged that urban planners deliberately "uglified" American cities, and portrayed brutalist architecture, graffiti, public drug use and violent crime as deliberate attacks on the public.
  5. Healthy: Carlson embraced RFK Jr.'s food agenda, called for universal sobriety and said widespread use of drugs such as Xanax, Adderall and SSRIs had left Americans "half-addled."
  6. Honest: Government officials should be punished for lying to citizens, and most classified records — including on the JFK assassination and 9/11 — should be opened.
  7. Optimistic: Carlson argued that having children is a biological imperative and the foundation of long-term thinking, while blaming aging and childless elites for policies that disregard future generations.
  8. Wise: Schools should teach how the physical world actually works and what he called unchanging facts about human nature — including innate differences between men and women — rather than credentials, screens and technological fads.
  9. Decent: The U.S. should apologize and pay restitution for killing noncombatants, reverse Trump's "Department of War" rebrand and stop funding allies that commit what Carlson called genocide, citing Israel.
  10. United: Carlson called for halting immigration until the effects of AI become clearer, ending benefits for undocumented immigrants and making English the sole language of federal documents and ballots.

The big picture: Carlson has become the intellectual hub for a small but vocal faction of MAGA exiles who say Trump abandoned the "America First" agenda by launching the Iran war, mishandling the Epstein files and allowing Israel to exert too much influence over U.S. policy.

  • The loose group includes former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, Rep. Thomas Massie and Joe Kent, who resigned as Trump's counterterrorism chief in March to protest the war.
  • The White House dismissed them as an "embarrassing collection of mostly whiny turncoats who dramatically overestimate their influence and relevance," while declaring Trump the "unequivocal leader" of the Republican Party.

Tucker Carlson used a highly promoted livestream Wednesday to unveil a 10-point vision for America — defining the worldview of a breakaway MAGA faction increasingly at odds with President Trump.

Why it matters: After vowing last month to "help build a third party," Carlson fueled further speculation this weekend by hosting MAGA dissidents at his home in Maine, where they urged him to run for president in 2028.

  • The former Fox News host stopped short of a formal launch, instead presenting the manifesto as the foundation for "whatever comes next" — a new political order he said could "find all kinds of expressions."

Zoom in: Carlson said any successor to America's faltering political system should begin with a shared understanding of what the country "should be," which he distilled into 10 points.

  1. Fair: The same rules should apply to presidents, federal agents and elites such as Jeffrey Epstein, whose impunity Carlson cast as emblematic of an "Epstein class" enriching itself through a corrupt system.
  2. Sovereign: Carlson claimed Israel pushed the U.S. into the Iran war through "bribery or threat or both," while describing foreign lobbying, corporate control of government and high-interest debt as forms of "slavery."
  3. Productive: America should rebuild farming, manufacturing and craftsmanship while rejecting an economy dominated by finance, real estate speculation, surveillance systems and weapons.
  4. Beautiful: Carlson alleged that urban planners deliberately "uglified" American cities, and portrayed brutalist architecture, graffiti, public drug use and violent crime as deliberate attacks on the public.
  5. Healthy: Carlson embraced RFK Jr.'s food agenda, called for universal sobriety and said widespread use of drugs such as Xanax, Adderall and SSRIs had left Americans "half-addled."
  6. Honest: Government officials should be punished for lying to citizens, and most classified records — including on the JFK assassination and 9/11 — should be opened.
  7. Optimistic: Carlson argued that having children is a biological imperative and the foundation of long-term thinking, while blaming aging and childless elites for policies that disregard future generations.
  8. Wise: Schools should teach how the physical world actually works and what he called unchanging facts about human nature — including innate differences between men and women — rather than credentials, screens and technological fads.
  9. Decent: The U.S. should apologize and pay restitution for killing noncombatants, reverse Trump's "Department of War" rebrand and stop funding allies that commit what Carlson called genocide, citing Israel.
  10. United: Carlson called for halting immigration until the effects of AI become clearer, ending benefits for undocumented immigrants and making English the sole language of federal documents and ballots.

The big picture: Carlson has become the intellectual hub for a small but vocal faction of MAGA exiles who say Trump abandoned the "America First" agenda by launching the Iran war, mishandling the Epstein files and allowing Israel to exert too much influence over U.S. policy.

  • The loose group includes former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, Rep. Thomas Massie and Joe Kent, who resigned as Trump's counterterrorism chief in March to protest the war.
  • The White House dismissed them as an "embarrassing collection of mostly whiny turncoats who dramatically overestimate their influence and relevance," while declaring Trump the "unequivocal leader" of the Republican Party.

item.title: Trump deportations cost taxpayers $2,358 each
item.description:
Data: Economic Policy Institute; Map: Danielle Alberti/Axios

American taxpayers would pay about $2,358 each for President Trump's mass deportation push, according to a new calculator tool from the Economic Policy Institute.

Why it matters: The estimate fuels debate over whether billions of federal dollars devoted to deportations could instead fund other public priorities such as food assistance, health care or housing.

By the numbers: EPI estimates the $268.9 billion projected for deportations could alternatively fund more than 118 million additional SNAP recipients over the remaining 2.5 years of the Trump administration, based on National Priorities Project data.

  • Alternatively, nearly 12 million additional people could receive Medicaid.
  • Or more than 9.7 million households could gain access to low-cost public housing.

What they're saying: "I don't think people realize how much money is being spent on these mass deportations," Gordon Lafer, a professor at the University of Oregon's Labor Education and Research Center and research associate at EPI, tells Axios.

  • "In almost every place in the country, there a lot of people who are struggling to not be hungry, to have affordable housing, kids are in overcrowded classrooms, people don't have health insurance, and those are the things that matter most."
  • "Instead, we're spending an unbelievable amount of money, chasing down, detaining, deporting people," he said, noting that most undocumented people lack criminal records. "It costs money that is desperately needed for other things in almost every community in the country."

The other side: A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson blamed the Biden administration in a statement to Axios for ignoring the costs of illegal immigration and said the administration's self-deportation program saves taxpayers money.

  • The spokesperson encouraged undocumented immigrants to use the CBP Home app, saying the U.S. offers a free flight and a $2,600 stipend to self-deport. The statement said that brings the cost of a self-deportation to about $5,100, saving taxpayers more than $13,000 per person compared with traditional deportation.

Zoom in: EPI estimated each area's share of federal income taxes to calculate how much taxpayers in each state, county and city would contribute toward deportation spending.

  • Areas that contribute a larger share of federal income taxes would shoulder a larger share of the projected cost.
  • Washington, D.C., taxpayers could pay $3,930 each. That amount could instead fund SNAP benefits for 455,000 additional people, public housing assistance for 21,000 households or Medicaid coverage for 30,000 people.
  • In a small state like Connecticut, taxpayers could pay $3,395 per person. According to the analysis, that amount could alternatively fund SNAP benefits for 1.9 million Connecticuters, public housing assistance for roughly 181,000 households or Medicaid coverage for 186,000 people.sh

Yes, but: Taxpayers in states that contribute less in federal income taxes would pay less.

  • In West Virginia, for example, taxpayers could pay about $1,297 each.
  • That amount could instead fund SNAP benefits for 328,000 people, public housing assistance for 46,000 households or Medicaid coverage for 31,000 people.

Context: The $268.9 billion the administration is slated to spend over the course of Trump's second term on deportations is from a combination of money from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, budget reconciliation bills, regular appropriations and other repurposed funds.

  • DHS previously told Axios in July that the government spends roughly $18,000 per non-voluntary deportation.

What's next: If Congress approves additional funding through the appropriations process or other avenues, total deportation spending would increase.

Go deeper: How Trump's "self-deportation" push has ramped up

Editor's note: This story has been updated with DHS comment.

item.title: Trump Marine One flight under investigation after potential safety mishap
item.description:
Federal aviation officials are investigating an air-safety incident involving President Trump's Marine One helicopter in Washington, D.C.

Why it matters: The incident comes as regulators work to improve safety in increasingly congested U.S. airspace, particularly around the nation's capital.

Zoom in: The Wall Street Journal first reported that the helicopter was carrying Trump on Tuesday when it flew too close to a commercial airliner departing from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

  • The National Transportation Safety Board confirmed in a statement to Axios that it is "investigating a reported loss of separation event" between the two aircraft.

A spokesperson for the Federal Aviation Administration said the agency is reviewing the incident.

  • "Based on our preliminary safety review, there was momentary loss of separation after which the aircraft continued to move away from one another," he said.
  • "The air traffic controller was in contact with both the commercial pilot and Marine One pilot during the loss of separation," he said, adding that "the president was never in danger."

Context: The FAA placed permanent restrictions and banned mixed helicopter and jet traffic around the Reagan National following a fatal midair collision in January 2025.

What they're saying: "Although the president was at no point in harm's way during yesterday's momentary loss of separation, the White House continues to work with relevant military, FAA and other security personnel to ensure the president's continued safety," White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in a statement.

Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

item.title: Chuck Edwards' abrupt exit leaves Republicans scrambling
item.description:
For Speaker Mike Johnson, Rep. Chuck Edwards' decision to drop his re-election bid just trades one problem for another. Why it matters: Instead of trying to hold a vulnerable seat with a scandal-ridden candidate, Republicans now have to scramble for a replacement who'll be starting at square one three months out from Election Day against a well-funded Democrat.

  • North Carolina's 11th District already was in Democrats' sights long before Edwards became the target of a House Ethics probe this spring — and things were not trending Republicans' way.
  • Sabato's Crystal Ball shifted the race from "lean Republican" to "toss-up" last Thursday, after Edwards' Democratic opponent, Jamie Ager, significantly outraised him in the second quarter.
  • Then the House Ethics Committee concluded Monday that Edwards violated House rules over sexual harassment and creating a hostile work environment based on his conduct toward female staffers — and recommended his censure.

After Edwards abruptly dropped out via social media very early this morning, GOP operatives privately acknowledged the seat was in trouble — and the late shakeup has only weakened their position.

  • One North Carolina Republican told Axios that Edwards had already "soured" the party's chances of holding the seat.

Zoom in: National Republicans will be forced to pour money into the race, as the replacement nominee will have to quickly build a campaign from the ground up.

  • Ager is already fundraising off Edwards' abrupt exit, texting supporters Wednesday: "Our Republican opponent dropped out today. While we don't know yet who we'll face in November, we need to be prepared for anything. Political experts have called this race a 𝙏𝙊𝙎𝙎-𝙐𝙋 so this seat will be critical to flip the House blue."

Driving the news: "After much prayer and reflection, I've decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign. I will complete my current term," Edwards wrote in a 3:32am ET post on X.

  • The ethics panel's findings corroborated several incidents first reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings and casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings.

Between the lines: Republicans are also bracing for Democrats to try to force a vote on expelling Edwards, a move that could further complicate the GOP's narrow House majority.

  • Edwards is likely to be censured when the House returns from its August recess, and the vote is expected to garner broad bipartisan support.
  • The House Democratic Women's Caucus called on Edwards to resign Monday, arguing that censure "has no real consequences," Axios first reported.
  • Democrats also see an opportunity to keep attention on the case as they push for tougher penalties for lawmakers found to have engaged in sexual misconduct.

Zoom out: Edwards is just the latest House Republican whose ethics troubles have complicated what should have been a relatively safe reelection campaign.

  • Reps. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) and Max Miller (R-Ohio) have also put otherwise comfortable seats into play for Democrats over their own scandals.

What's next: The Executive Committee of North Carolina's 11th District will meet Monday at 6:30pm to choose a replacement nominee, according to an email obtained by Axios.

  • North Carolina Republicans are increasingly coalescing around state Sen. Tim Moffitt as Edwards' replacement.
  • Some Republicans who had been eyeing the seat are shying away, worried about the abbreviated campaign and increasingly difficult political environment.

item.title: 2026 is turning into a bloodbath for safe-seat House Democrats
item.description:
A half dozen House Democrats in safe districts have lost their primaries so far this election cycle — and many more could soon follow suit.

Why it matters: Many of these losses are the result of growing restlessness among the Democratic grassroots that has increasingly morphed into anger towards the party establishment.

  • "I expected a lot of people to run because they didn't know how to respond to Trump without just being active," Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.) told Axios.
  • He added: "We're seeing that and all the primary electorate voting right now."

Driving the news: Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.) on Wednesday became the latest incumbent to fall short in his primary, losing to state Rep. Donavan McKinney despite a heavy spending advantage.

  • Thanedar — like nearly all Democratic incumbents — was backed by House Democratic leadership, as well as the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the center-left New Democrat Coalition.
  • McKinney had support from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) and left-wing groups including Justice Democrats, the Democratic Socialists of America and the Working Families Party.

Yes, but: While that primary was, on the surface, a battle between the establishment and the left, House Democrats cautioned not to read too much into the result.

  • Thanedar "didn't do his job," said one senior House Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to give candid comments about a colleague.
  • "He didn't deliver constituent services. All he did was talk about himself."

The big picture: Thanedar joins Reps. Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.), Diana DeGette (D-Colo.) and Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.), who were all unseated by challengers running to their left.

  • Freshman Rep. Christian Menefee (D-Texas) defeated longtime Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) after the two were drawn into a district together.
  • And Rep. Julie Johnson (D-Texas) lost her primary to former Rep. Colin Allred.

By the numbers: This is one of just four election cycles since 1994 in which at least half a dozen House Democrats have lost their primaries.

  • The other three cycles — 2002, 2012 and 2022 — all came after congressional reapportionment, which often pits incumbent House members against one another.
  • Only one Democratic primary ouster this year — Green's loss to Menefee — has been the result of mid-decade redistricting.
Data: Axios research; Note: The 2026 cycle is still ongoing; Chart: Andrew Solender/Axios

What's next: Plenty more hurdles await Democratic incumbents, particularly those 70 and older who have had lengthy tenures in Congress.

  • Rep. John Larson (D-Conn.) is trying to fend off a serious challenge from former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, while Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.) is facing a challenge from attorney Patrick Roath.
  • Rep. Ed Case (D-Hawaii) is facing a spirited challenge from state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole.
  • Reps. Doris Matsui (D-Calif.) and Mike Thompson (D-Calif.) are both facing Democratic challengers in their November runoffs.

The left is also hoping to unseat Reps. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) and Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.), as well as Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.), who is facing criticism for running in a plurality Black district.

The bottom line: Pocan said the Democratic primary electorate's anti-incumbency energy is "a good thing ultimately, because people will be ready for November and ready for change."

  • "If we are talking to [voters] and respecting them," he added. "I think that's yet to be figured out if people are doing it correctly."

item.title: Senate confirms Schwartz for CDC director
item.description:
The Senate confirmed Erica Schwartz for Centers for Disease Control director on Wednesday, giving the beleaguered agency its first full-time political leader in almost a year.

Why it matters: While the 51-44 vote marked a step toward refilling the depleted ranks of the Trump administration's health care leadership, it didn't fully resolve questions about whether Schwartz could steer clear of political interference.

Driving the news: Just one Democrat — Sen. Tim Kaine (Va.) — supported Schwartz's nomination, along with all of the Republicans present.

  • "She's got the qualifications for the job," Kaine told Politico last week after voting to advance Schwartz's nomination out of committee. Schwartz is a physician who worked at the Department of Health and Human Services during the first Trump administration.
  • Senate health committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who had been skeptical of Schwartz, said he decided to support her after being assured through their conversations that "she knows what she is doing and will stand against those who do not."

Context: Schwartz faced tough questioning during her July 15 confirmation hearing over whether she could chart a course for the public health agency and work with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

  • She vowed to rebuild trust in the CDC but hedged on whether she would tell Congress if she was told to adopt "unscientific" or harmful policies, saying she didn't believe either President Trump or Kennedy would do that.
  • Many public health leaders initially applauded her nomination, but some said they could not support Schwartz after her confirmation hearing, saying she failed to give clear answers to simple questions.

Schwartz was Trump's third nominee to lead the CDC, following Susan Monarez, who was fired after less than a month in the role. She claimed she was dismissed for refusing to rubber-stamp Kennedy's vaccine policies.

  • The former deputy surgeon general was viewed as a less polarizing pick. But policy experts say she'll face challenges stabilizing an agency that's lacked a full-time political leader for almost a year and is beset by morale and staffing problems.

The Senate hasn't yet scheduled a vote on whether to confirm Sean Kaufman for HHS assistant health secretary for preparedness and response.

  • Kaufman also seems poised to get confirmed, despite lingering questions about past anti-vaccine statements.
  • Before the health committee approved Kaufman's nomination last month, Cassidy said he got a few concessions from HHS to justify his support, including "key personnel changes" — which he never specified — and assurances that Kaufman won't be involved in vaccine policy.

  • Many public health leaders initially applauded her nomination, but some said they could not support Schwartz after her confirmation hearing, saying she failed to give clear answers to simple questions.

Schwartz was Trump's third nominee to lead the CDC, following Susan Monarez, who was fired after less than a month in the role. She claimed she was dismissed for refusing to rubber-stamp Kennedy's vaccine policies.

  • The former deputy surgeon general was viewed as a less polarizing pick. But policy experts say she'll face challenges stabilizing an agency that's lacked a full-time political leader for almost a year and is beset by morale and staffing problems.

The Senate hasn't yet scheduled a vote on whether to confirm Sean Kaufman for HHS assistant health secretary for preparedness and response.

  • Kaufman also seems poised to get confirmed, despite lingering questions about past anti-vaccine statements.
  • Before the health committee approved Kaufman's nomination last month, Cassidy said he got a few concessions from HHS to justify his support, including "key personnel changes" — which he never specified — and assurances that Kaufman won't be involved in vaccine policy.

item.title: DOJ's voter roll crusade hits a courthouse wall
item.description:
Federal judges, appointed by both Democrats and Republicans, have handed the Justice Department a steady stream of losses in the administration's attempt to obtain sensitive voter information.

Why it matters: The DOJ has sued 30 U.S. states, as well as D.C., for rebuffing its demands, all to back President Trump's efforts to reshape voting after years of spreading unproven claims of massive fraud.

The latest: U.S. District Judge Philip Brimmer, a George W. Bush appointee, sided with Colorado in dismissing the DOJ's case against the Democratic secretary of state with prejudice Monday.

  • The administration argued that provisions in the Civil Rights Act of 1960 gave the attorney general "sweeping power" to obtain the sought-after records, which included registrants' driver's license numbers and the last four digits of their Social Security identifier.
  • But Brimmer concluded that compelling the release of the state's voter lists did not fall under that authority.

By the numbers: He's not alone: Judges in 20 cases, per the Brennan Center for Justice's tracker, have rebuked the DOJ in a consistent losing streak.

  • A judge in California called the request "unprecedented and illegal." In Rhode Island, a Trump appointee named it a "fishing expedition."
  • And in June, a U.S. appeals court joined the growing body of federal judges ruling against the DOJ, handing the administration its first appellate-level loss in its campaign.

The other side: Meanwhile, more than a dozen states have agreed to share the data the administration is seeking — while others agreed only to provide data that is publicly available.

Zoom out: The DOJ's quest for voter information is far from the only election pressure the administration has put on states. But it hasn't been all smooth sailing on those fronts, either.

  • Trump has claimed hundreds of thousands of unauthorized immigrants are on voting rolls in key states — but the numbers the Department of Homeland Security has publicized in four states (all of which refused to hand over voter rolls) have baffled election officials, NPR reported.
  • He's pushed hard on a proof-of-citizenship voting bill, the SAVE America Act, but its future in the Senate remains murky.
  • And his push to restrict mail-in voting, which has hit legal headwinds, could be heading to the Supreme Court.

Between the lines: The broad sweep approach to obtaining voter info isn't shaping up for the administration; some of the information has been received in other ways.

  • ICE investigators obtained individual voter files in at least two counties — one in Texas and one in North Carolina.
  • And the FBI recently obtained the IP address of someone who completed their voter registration online in South Carolina, Axios' Brittany Gibson reports.

Go deeper: America gripped by election fears as November nears

item.title: Employers are hiring less but paying more
item.description:
Private employment data suggests that the labor market might be tighter than the headline hiring numbers alone suggest, with worker pay accelerating alongside lackluster jobs growth.

Why it matters: Employers are pulling back on hiring as they navigate an uncertain economic outlook, but supply constraints continue to limit the pool of available workers in some industries.

  • That's helping speed up pay growth — a boon for workers in industries like construction and health care, where employers are still competing for scarce labor.
  • But the labor market is becoming increasingly uneven: While employers in some sectors are paying up to attract workers, others are more cautious about hiring as they contend with geopolitical uncertainty, tariffs and a more reluctant consumer.

What they're saying: "Pay is reflecting a labor market that is not getting looser, but maybe tightening a little bit. What you're seeing is pockets of supply constraints," ADP chief economist Nela Richardson told reporters Wednesday morning.

  • "There is a mix of supply and demand drivers," she added. That means "a strong month or a weak month may just be a short-term change in a hiring pattern, rather than a longer-term signal" about the labor market's health.

By the numbers: Private employers added just 44,000 jobs in July, down from 95,000 in June and the weakest monthly gain since January, according to ADP.

  • But annual pay growth for workers who changed jobs accelerated to 7%, the fastest pace since August 2025, while pay for workers who stayed put held steady at 4.4%.
  • Construction added just 1,000 jobs in July, but pay for construction workers changing jobs is at a record high, reflecting strong demand from AI-related data center construction and a limited supply of experienced workers, Richardson said.
  • Education and health services led all industries with 36,000 new jobs last month. Even though pay growth there is not as eye-popping as it is in construction, it remains elevated as employers continue to compete for a limited pool of workers, Richardson noted.

Between the lines: Other private-sector data shows that the labor market remains more resilient than the headline hiring figures alone suggest.

  • The Bank of America Institute on Wednesday morning said its payroll gauge, based on customer deposit account data, accelerated to 2% year-over-year in July from 1.7% in June, with hiring strongest among lower-income workers.

The intrigue: The bank also said that after-tax wage growth for lower-income households accelerated to 5.2% last month, surpassing pay growth of higher-income households for the first time since late 2024.

  • "This is a convergence, but it's an upward convergence," Bank of America Institute senior economist David Tinsley told reporters. "It's not that everything is leveling down — it seems to be more of a leveling up in the data right now."
  • Tinsley said that the data points to "some evidence of tightening overall" in the labor market, as labor supply remains constrained and employers continue to compete for workers.

The bottom line: Some employers are reluctant to hire, but persistent worker shortages are keeping wage pressures alive in key industries.

  • Tinsley said that firmer wage growth does not necessarily mean that the labor force is a source of inflationary pressure, noting that whether higher pay translates into inflation depends in part on productivity gains.
  • ADP's Richardson said that the pay growth pickup is worth watching, but "I don't think that's enough to tip into an inflationary cycle."

item.title: Rep. Chuck Edwards drops re-election bid after censure recommendation
item.description:
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) dropped his re-election bid early Wednesday after the House Ethics Committee concluded he violated House rules over sexual harassment and creating a hostile work environment, and recommended his censure.

  • The findings follow Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two young female staffers in their 20s for special attention that multiple sources described as inappropriate.

Why it matters: Pressure has been mounting on Edwards to step aside since the Ethics Committee released its report Monday, amid mounting concerns that Democrats could flip his seat in November.

  • "After much prayer and reflection, I've decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign. I will complete my current term," Edwards wrote in a 3:32 a.m. ET post on X.
  • The ethics panel's findings corroborated several incidents first reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, and casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings.

Driving the news: Ethics found that Edwards violated House rules by "failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers."

  • Edwards has consistently denied wrongdoing.
  • In a 15-page rebuttal to the Ethics report, Edwards' attorneys called the committee's conclusions "unfounded."

Between the lines: Democratic challenger Jamie Ager has significantly outraised Edwards, and a censure on Edwards' record would have further complicated his reelection prospects.

  • Sabato's Crystal Ball shifted Edwards' reelection race in North Carolina's 11th District from "lean Republican" to "toss-up" last Thursday.

Zoom in: The House had been expected to vote on censuring Edwards after returning from the August recess, with Republicans indicating this week that the effort would likely succeed.

  • Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) told Axios on Monday that she would vote to censure Edwards. "Sexual harassment is completely unacceptable," Luna said.
  • A House GOP leadership aide told Axios before he announced his resignation they "don't see a path" where Edwards avoids censure.
  • The House Democratic Women's caucus called on Edwards to resign Monday, arguing that censure "has no real consequences," Axios first reported.

Behind the scenes: House Republican leadership urged Edwards to drop his reelection bid following the Ethics report, two sources told Axios.

  • When asked if Edwards should drop out Tuesday night, Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told Politico, "He's got to make a big decision, and I hope he does the right thing for him and his family."
  • Republicans still expect that Edwards will be censured when the House returns from the August recess.

What's next: The Executive Committee of North Carolina's 11th District will meet Monday at 6:30 pm at the Buncombe County Headquarters to choose a replacement nominee, according to an email obtained by Axios sent from North Carolina's 11th Congressional District Chair Merry Guy.

  • District and county officers, appointed officials, committee members and additional members elected at the convention will all vote on the replacement.
  • State Sens. Tim Moffitt and Kevin Corbin, and state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom are all being discussed as possible candidates, according two sources familiar with the process.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.

item.title: Rep. Thanedar loses to socialist McKinney in Democratic primary for congress
item.description:
State Rep. Donavan McKinney bested two-term incumbent Rep. Shri Thanedar in Tuesday's Democratic primary to represent Michigan's 13th Congressional District.

Why it matters: The lifelong Detroiter's win likely returns Detroit to Black representation in Congress, which ended with Thanedar's 2022 victory.

  • It also brings another victory for a progressive-backed candidate.
  • McKinney won by a slim 51.9% to 48.1%, with the race called late Wednesday morning by AP.

State of play: Thanedar had the advantage on funding and name recognition. However, mainstream House Democrats didn't seem as concerned about him losing to a progressive challenger as in other races, Axios' Andrew Solender reports.

Yes, but: McKinney still needs to win in November to head to Congress, but defeat is unlikely in the heavily blue district.

  • The district includes most of Detroit and extends westward past Taylor.

Between the lines: Both candidates campaigned against Trump, criticized ICE and supported expanding access to health care.

  • Thanedar, a wealthy businessman who largely self-funds his campaigns, was backed by AIPAC, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and both the Congressional Progressive Caucus and center-left New Democrat Coalition.
  • But McKinney won the endorsement of local institutions like the Michigan Chronicle and labor groups, as well as national-level progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Rashida Tlaib and former Rep. Brenda Lawrence.

The bottom line: The race was more nuanced than representing the ideological divisions in the Democratic Party.

  • Factors at play included McKinney's deep connections to Detroit, state legislative record, questions about Thanedar's effectiveness and the prospect of restoring Detroit's Black representation in Congress.

item.title: Three Michigan races put the progressive movement's reach on display
item.description:
Michigan progressives woke up Wednesday after a banner night: Abdul El-Sayed overcame an outsized cash advantage in the Democratic Senate primary, Will Lawrence won a battleground House nomination, and Donavan McKinney ousted Rep. Shri Thanedar.

  • Why it matters: The sweep signals the left's growing strength in a key swing state.
  • The state's Democratic Socialists of America chapters, the Working Families Party and the United Auto Workers all flexed their muscles Tuesday up and down the ballot.

State of play: El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, clung to a narrow lead over four-term Rep. Haley Stevens — 48.5%–47.5% with 99% of the vote counted. He will face Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan's open Senate seat, a must-win for Democrats hoping to gain Senate control.

  • Lawrence, a Sunrise Movement co-founder, upset Bridget Brink, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine and Matt Maasdam, a former Navy SEAL, winning the 7th district nomination by 15 points. Lawrence will try to flip the swing seat held by GOP Rep. Tom Barrett.
  • State Rep. McKinney, a Democratic Socialists of America member backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), defeated Thanedar 51.9%–48.1% in a solidly blue seat. Thanedar is the latest House Democrat toppled by the left.

The big picture: The bitter and expensive campaign became the most notable proxy battle between the Democratic Party's establishment and progressive wings.

  • El-Sayed has said he's not a democratic socialist, but many DSA members have backed him.

Zoom in: The left saw even more victories downballot, with a DSA member ousting an incumbent state representative, a cofounder of the Uncommitted Movement nominated in a state senate race and a Working Families Party-endorsed candidate set to win an open state house seat.

  • A socialist was also named the Democratic nominee in Ann Arbor's mayoral race and is unopposed in November.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: Left turn in Michigan: Tuesday's primary takeaways
item.description:
Progressives scored their biggest win of the year Tuesday in Michigan's Senate primary, narrowly defeating the Democratic establishment in the clearest sign yet of how a populist surge is remaking the party.

Why it matters: Left-wing outsider Abdul El-Sayed underperformed predictions, but his victory over moderate Rep. Haley Stevens was still a rebuke to party leaders in D.C. and Michigan, and to big donors who flooded Stevens' campaign with cash.

  • El-Sayed was outspent 9 to 1 by Stevens and her allies — including AIPAC's political arm. He ran on an unapologetically progressive platform to abolish ICE, support Medicare for All and staunchly oppose aid to Israel.
  • In a bitter campaign, El-Sayed was painted as a sexist, an antisemite and critic of former First Lady Michelle Obama — much of it on the airwaves. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer cut a slick video backing Stevens.
  • It wasn't enough.

Key takeaways from Michigan:

1. Progressives lay the groundwork for 2028.

  • Progressives and democratic socialists have been eager to show that one of their own can carry a battleground state that will be crucial in the next presidential election. They'll get a chance to prove that in November, now that El-Sayed has been nominated in Michigan.
  • If El-Sayed succeeds in November, it'll be seen as a boon for the prospects of a left-wing 2028 presidential contender such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
  • On the other hand, if El-Sayed were to stumble, AOC — who's mulling a run for Senate or the White House in 2028 — likely would share some of the backlash. She's been among El-Sayed's top surrogates.

2. Bernie hands Chuck an "L."

  • With the progressive movement he'd fostered for so long building unprecedented momentum, progressive icon and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders went on a mission to elect progressives up and down the ticket this year — often opposing Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's favorites, including Stevens.
  • Sanders backed El-Sayed on the first day of his campaign. Stevens' loss marks the second time this year that Schumer failed to get his preferred candidate over the finish line in a Senate primary. The last time the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee whiffed in a major primary before this year was in 2010.

3. Money isn't everything.

  • El-Sayed, a former a former Wayne County health director, compared himself to David going up against Goliath.
  • The Biblical allusion made many moderate Democrats roll their eyes, but the spending disparity in the race was truly enormous: Stevens and her allies spent $65 million on ads compared to $7.5 million by El-Sayed and his supporters, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
  • Stevens' loss is a large face-plant for AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobby whose super PAC poured more than $30 million into the race against El-Sayed. The results could lead more Democrats to distance themselves from AIPAC money at a time when Israel's image has nosedived among the party's voters.

4. Republicans like the result, too.

  • El-Sayed has excited the left, but many Republicans are happy with his win as well.
  • Recent polls have suggested that former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP's Senate nominee, would fare better against El-Sayed than Stevens. Trump already has branded El-Sayed a "communist," a theme voters can expect to hear from the GOP throughout the fall. (El-Sayed has said he's a capitalist, not a socialist.)
  • El-Sayed, meanwhile, faces the challenge of reuniting a deeply divided Democratic Party, wooing independent voters and trying to attract some Republicans.
  • Many centrist Democrats are skeptical he can pull it off — and point to Tuesday's closer-than-expected results as evidence he could lack enough big-tent appeal in November.

5. The left also shows its muscle in down-ballot races.

  • For progressives, it wasn't just El-Sayed: Will Lawrence won a battleground House nomination, and Donavan McKinney was threatening to oust Rep. Shri Thanedar.
  • Yousef Rabhi declared victory over incumbent Christopher Taylor in the Democratic primary for mayor in solidly blue Ann Arbor.
  • And Abbas Alawieh of Dearborn — cofounder of Uncommitted, a group formed to protest U.S. support of Israel — was ahead of state Rep. Erin Byrnes in the race for the Democratic nomination of a state Senate seat.

1. Progressives lay the groundwork for 2028.

  • Progressives and democratic socialists have been eager to show that one of their own can carry a battleground state that will be crucial in the next presidential election. They'll get a chance to prove that in November, now that El-Sayed has been nominated in Michigan.
  • If El-Sayed succeeds in November, it'll be seen as a boon for the prospects of a left-wing 2028 presidential contender such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
  • On the other hand, if El-Sayed were to stumble, AOC — who's mulling a run for Senate or the White House in 2028 — likely would share some of the backlash. She's been among El-Sayed's top surrogates.

2. Bernie hands Chuck an "L."

  • With the progressive movement he'd fostered for so long building unprecedented momentum, progressive icon and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders went on a mission to elect progressives up and down the ticket this year — often opposing Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's favorites, including Stevens.
  • Sanders backed El-Sayed on the first day of his campaign. Stevens' loss marks the second time this year that Schumer failed to get his preferred candidate over the finish line in a Senate primary. The last time the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee whiffed in a major primary before this year was in 2010.

3. Money isn't everything.

  • El-Sayed, a former a former Wayne County health director, compared himself to David going up against Goliath.
  • The Biblical allusion made many moderate Democrats roll their eyes, but the spending disparity in the race was truly enormous: Stevens and her allies spent $65 million on ads compared to $7.5 million by El-Sayed and his supporters, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
  • Stevens' loss is a large face-plant for AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobby whose super PAC poured more than $30 million into the race against El-Sayed. The results could lead more Democrats to distance themselves from AIPAC money at a time when Israel's image has nosedived among the party's voters.

4. Republicans like the result, too.

  • El-Sayed has excited the left, but many Republicans are happy with his win as well.
  • Recent polls have suggested that former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP's Senate nominee, would fare better against El-Sayed than Stevens. Trump already has branded El-Sayed a "communist," a theme voters can expect to hear from the GOP throughout the fall. (El-Sayed has said he's a capitalist, not a socialist.)
  • El-Sayed, meanwhile, faces the challenge of reuniting a deeply divided Democratic Party, wooing independent voters and trying to attract some Republicans.
  • Many centrist Democrats are skeptical he can pull it off — and point to Tuesday's closer-than-expected results as evidence he could lack enough big-tent appeal in November.

5. The left also shows its muscle in down-ballot races.

  • For progressives, it wasn't just El-Sayed: Will Lawrence won a battleground House nomination, and Donavan McKinney was threatening to oust Rep. Shri Thanedar.
  • Yousef Rabhi declared victory over incumbent Christopher Taylor in the Democratic primary for mayor in solidly blue Ann Arbor.
  • And Abbas Alawieh of Dearborn — cofounder of Uncommitted, a group formed to protest U.S. support of Israel — was ahead of state Rep. Erin Byrnes in the race for the Democratic nomination of a state Senate seat.

item.title: House Democrats pack 2026 target list with more Trump-won seats
item.description:
Data: The Downballot, Dave's Redistricting Atlas, The Texas Tribune; Table: Andrew Solender/Axios

House Democrats' campaign arm announced Wednesday it is adding a dozen districts that President Trump won handily in 2024 to their midterm target list.

Why it matters: The additions are meant to project Democratic confidence that they can compete in solidly Republican territory come November.

  • "House Democrats are expanding the battlefield deep into Trump terrain," Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee chair Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.) said in a statement.
  • Republicans aren't buying it. National Republican Congressional Committee spokesman Mike Marinella said the DCCC has "officially entered the hallucination phase of the election cycle."

Driving the news: In a news release shared with Axios, the DCCC announced the new additions to its "Districts in Play" list — which now includes 59 districts where the party thinks it has at least a narrow shot.

  • Trump easily carried all the new districts on the list in 2024, by margins ranging from roughly 10 percentage points in Colorado's 3rd district to a 21-point win in Tennessee's 9th.
  • The most provocative of the additions: North Carolina's 9th district, where NRCC chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) is facing a challenge from populist Democrat Richard Ojeda.

Reality check: The DCCC is not going to spend big money to try to compete in 59 Republican-held and open seats — the battlefield will be much smaller than that, likely no more than a few dozen districts.

  • The announcement is more a way to flex muscle about the national environment, with the press release citing CNN polling from last week that put congressional Democrats ahead by 8 points nationally.
  • "MAGA Republicans who historically have considered themselves 'safe' have let down the people they were elected to represent," DelBene said in her statement.

The other side: "Instead of explaining why radical socialists hijacked the districts they actually need to win, they're pretending deep-red Republican seats are suddenly competitive," Marinella said.

item.title: Investors can't stop believing
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Who cares about war, oil prices, interest rates or an AI bubble? Investors apparently do not — for now at least — sending stocks back to record highs.

Why it matters: High stock prices are critical to keeping funds flowing to the AI buildout.

  • A significant erosion of investors' confidence in stocks would be a big risk to the AI flywheel of financial flows, capital expenditures and industrial activity driving the U.S. economy.

Catch up quick: Some analysts and investors had worried that the markets were beginning to deflate, as the S&P 500 failed to advance in June or July.

  • Previously high-flying chip stocks hit an air pocket in early June.
  • The slump then spread to hyperscalers, with the Mag 7 stocks becoming the Lag 7.

The latest: In the last four sessions, however, stocks have jumped almost 6%, led by massive gains from some of those same tech giants after Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet each reported their quarterly results.

  • The S&P 500 rose 1.8% Tuesday, notching a new all-time closing high of 7736.52.
  • Tech shares led the way on Tuesday, as retail favorite Palantir Technologies soared 29.5% after its second-quarter results showed strong sales of its AI software platform to corporate clients.
  • Palantir's ability to profitably sell AI services appeared to help reinvigorate the AI trade, with semiconductor stocks and makers of other IT hardware that data centers need jumping.
  • American producers of components called transceivers — used to connect fiber optic cables that carry data — also rose after reports that the Trump administration was considering banning similar products from Chinese competitors on security grounds.

Context: The revival of tech momentum adds to the strength of so-called "cyclical" sectors of the stock market — such as industrial companies, financial firms and energy stocks — that have largely kept the S&P 500 from falling too much throughout the recent soft patch.

  • Energy shares — the benchmark index's biggest riser so far this year, up more than 30% — have of course been lifted by the Iran-related surge in oil prices.
  • But industrial stocks have also risen amid growing proof that cash from the AI boom — driven by an expectation of almost $800 billion of capital expenditures by hyperscalers this year, according to FactSet data — is working its way deep into the industrial tissue of the U.S. economy.
  • The S&P 500 industrials are up 20% year to date. If there at year end, it would be the best performance for the industrial sector since 2019.
Data: FactSet; Note: Expectations are for calendar year 2026, per FactSet. Hyperscalers include Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

The big picture: Indeed, the economy is looking hot by a number of measures, from surging capital goods orders to expanding manufacturing activity to growing demand for bank loans from bigger companies.

  • And corporate profits look, technically speaking, nutso high.

Caveat: You often hear Wall Street analysts describe this phenomenon as a "broadening out" of the AI boom, which has a nice, soothing ring to it.

  • Doesn't "broadening out" sound sort of like the "broad diversification" investors are supposed to seek out for market safety?

Yes, but: With AI now driving results at companies well beyond the tech sector, a skeptic might say that the market is actually more concentrated, rather than diversified, in terms of risk.

  • In other words, more and more of the U.S. economy seems to be reliant on this one gigantic gravy train to keep chugging. So far, it has.

The bottom line: The AI boom continues to roll, with more of the economy exposed to both the upside and the risk associated with one of the largest investment booms in American history.

item.title: Fauci's legal woes could deter scientists from government service
item.description:
Senate Republicans' planned vote this week on whether to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress is the latest escalation in their attempt to right perceived COVID-era wrongs and further disempower the federal health care bureaucracy.

Why it matters: Critics fear the Senate Homeland Security Committee's efforts will deter scientific talent from taking government jobs, weakening America's public health infrastructure and ceding its dominance in biomedical innovation.

Driving the news: The panel is expected to vote Thursday to hold the nation's former top infectious disease official in contempt for refusing to answer the committee's questions on the coronavirus during a hearing last week.

  • Fauci repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment in response to senators' questions and accused Chairman Rand Paul (R-Ky.) of having an "unhinged obsession with calling for my prosecution."
  • Paul has argued that the Fifth Amendment didn't apply to Fauci because he's already received a preemptive pardon from former President Biden covering all of his pandemic-era work.
  • All of this "has a chilling effect" on scientists considering future government work, top committee Democrat Gary Peters of Michigan told Axios. "You could be pulled before a committee and have every decision you make questioned in a hostile way."

The big picture: The panel's actions follow a broad hollowing out of the federal health workforce and efforts to assert more political control over career scientists.

  • The Department of Health and Human Services reduced its workforce from 82,000 full-time employees to 62,000 at the beginning of President Trump's second term.
  • Senior career health officials have also departed HHS and its subagencies on their own, with several publicly citing disagreement with leadership or a chaotic work environment.
  • Senate Republicans have signaled they may subpoena more government officials over their pandemic-era work, including Food and Drug Administration officials involved in COVID vaccine regulation.

What they're saying: "The government is becoming a less and less attractive place" to work, Ashish Jha, Biden's COVID response coordinator and former dean of the Brown University School of Public Health, told Axios.

  • "Now, we're essentially trying to criminalize government scientists giving advice to political leaders, if that is advice the political leaders don't like or it creates an outcome the political leaders didn't want."

The intrigue: The administration has also taken aim at federal research funding, most recently proposing a sweeping new regulation that would give political appointees the final say over the awarding of discretionary grants.

  • A bipartisan Senate bill that would fund the government through mid-December would block that change from taking effect through Dec. 11.

The other side: Republicans argue that holding a bad actor accountable — which is what they say they're doing with Fauci — shouldn't deter scrupulous scientists from government service.

  • "I hope everybody takes a look at really how dastardly Fauci performed throughout the pandemic. He was the anti-science," Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) said.
  • "It shouldn't if you're honest," Johnson replied when asked whether the committee's actions will have a chilling effect on the workforce.

And for some, weakening reliance on experts — or in the parlance of Republicans, unelected bureaucrats — is the goal, not an unintended consequence.

  • "Now we know that Anthony Fauci, who was the expert, was lying about everything, about masks, about the social distancing, about natural immunity, about the transmission from the vaccine, about the source of COVID," Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a fiery exchange with CNN's Dana Bash last weekend.
  • "He was lying, and you were punishing people for not trusting the experts. And now you're rolling out the experts again."

What we're watching: It may not take long to assess any impact on government hiring.

  • The administration is trying to recruit top talent to fill openings, including FDA commissioner and top drug and vaccine regulatory positions.

The bottom line: "If you undermine government capacity to do scientific work, you end up with a government that is far less capable of doing scientific work," Jha said.

item.title: Trump's golden age reality check
item.description:
The Trump administration's rosy promises of a new "golden age" with 6% economic growth have fizzled on the realities of slower-than-anticipated growth and souring consumer sentiment.

Why it matters: President Trump's roller coaster economy has risen with consumer spending and AI investment but also tumbled on tariff uncertainty, stubborn inflation and his Iran war, muddling the economic picture.

  • Trump preaches a golden future, but many voters aren't buying it.
  • That's a warning sign for the midterms: Reuters-Ipsos polling out this week found that Americans favored Democrats over Republicans on economic policy for the first time in nearly a decade.

The big picture: Roughly 18 months into Trump's second term, the economy has proved more resilient than many expected, buoyed in large part by an AI infrastructure buildout that transcends Washington politics.

  • But the dramatic acceleration the administration promised has yet to materialize.
  • Many economists believe the administration's most ambitious growth targets would require a productivity boom well beyond anything currently visible in the data.

Reality check: The economy grew at a 1.5% annualized rate in the second quarter, slowing from the 2.1% pace in the first quarter.

  • The economy has grown at roughly a 2% annualized pace since the start of 2025.
  • That's a solid pace, but it's little different from the economy's long-run trend and well short of the growth rates some of Trump's top economic officials have hyped in recent months.

Flashback: If you asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in January, growth could have hit 5% in the first quarter — even 6%, if the Fed cut interest rates, he said — which didn't happen.

  • Top White House economist Kevin Hassett pitched up to 6% growth back in the spring, attributing the boost to a future factory boom.
  • After back-to-back quarters of roughly 4% growth in the middle of 2025 — boosted in part by swings in trade tied to tariffs — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called the performance a "harbinger of what's to come."
  • Bessent's "3-3-3" economic blueprint targets sustained 3% annual growth.

Yes, but: The Congressional Budget Office estimates potential GDP growth will average about 2% over the next decade.

  • The last time the economy expanded at rates consistent with Trump officials' high-end predictions was during the one-off reopening from the pandemic.
  • "That's just unrealistic," says Michael Klein, an economics professor at Tuft University's Fletcher School and executive editor of EconoFact. "You don't see that in an economy like the United States."

What they're saying: Joseph Lavorgna, a former advisor to Bessent, says 3% growth is plausible, arguing the latest 1.5% GDP print didn't "fully … capture the robustness in the economy."

  • Underlying demand — stripping out volatile swings in trade, inventories and government spending — grew at a 3.9% annualized pace in the second quarter, thanks to strong consumer and business spending.
  • When Fox Business' Maria Bartiromo pressed Hassett Friday on his recent prediction of 4% growth in the second half of the year, Hassett argued he was discussing domestic demand rather than the topline number.
  • White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in a statement that "[d]espite possible inventories data lags, the Q2 GDP report reinforces … that the American consumer remains resilient and the long-term restoration of America's industrial base continues."

What to watch: The Trump administration on Monday touted a "nowcast" produced by the Atlanta Fed, which currently estimates growth is running at a robust 6% annualized pace in the current quarter.

  • But economists treat that figure with caution this early in the quarter: the model is still working with only a limited set of July economic data, and the estimate can change sharply as more reports are released.
  • At roughly the same point in the second quarter it was estimating growth of about 3.5% — more than double the 1.5% pace the economy ultimately posted.

Between the lines: Lavorgna tells Axios he "can't get there on the arithmetic" to 4% or 5% growth, noting that with a stagnant workforce, there'd have to be a significant boost in productivity to get there without inflation.

  • "The dynamics aren't going to allow us to grow at those growth rates, at least for the foreseeable future," he says.

Go deeper: U.S. economy grows at 1.5% rate in second quarter

item.title: Progressive Will Lawrence wins key Michigan House primary in blow to Dem leaders
item.description:
Sunrise Movement co-founder Will Lawrence is the latest progressive candidate to notch an upset Democratic House primary win — this time in a key battleground district in Michigan.

Why it matters: The seat is a top target for Democrats in November, but party leaders fear that Lawrence's left-leaning politics will make it much harder to win.

  • Several top House Democratic moderates expressed the view to Axios last month that Lawrence cannot beat Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.) in Michigan's 7th District.
  • But progressives have pushed back, arguing that concerns about Lawrence's viability in the general election are based on an outmoded metric of electability.

Driving the news: Lawrence defeated Bridget Brink, a former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine, and Matt Maasdam, a former Navy SEAL and military aide to President Obama, the Associated Press projected Tuesday night.

  • The outcome is what party leaders in both Michigan and D.C. had feared for weeks — that Maasdam and Brink would split the moderate vote and create an opening for Lawrence to win.
  • The race split the establishment down the middle, with the Democratic Women's Caucus backing Brink while Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) threw her support behind Maasdam.

Zoom out: Lawrence is one of several progressives who have beaten more establishment-aligned candidates in key swing districts this election cycle.

  • Progressive activist and political science professor Randy Villegas beat moderate California State Assemblymember Jasmeet Bains in the race to take on Rep. David Valadao (R-Calif.).
  • In Maine, progressive state Auditor Matt Dunlap won a primary victory over establishment-backed Joe Baldacci in the seat of retiring Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine).
  • The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee backed Bains and Baldacci but did not take a side in Michigan's 7th District.
item.content:encoded:
Sunrise Movement co-founder Will Lawrence is the latest progressive candidate to notch an upset Democratic House primary win — this time in a key battleground district in Michigan.

Why it matters: The seat is a top target for Democrats in November, but party leaders fear that Lawrence's left-leaning politics will make it much harder to win.

  • Several top House Democratic moderates expressed the view to Axios last month that Lawrence cannot beat Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.) in Michigan's 7th District.
  • But progressives have pushed back, arguing that concerns about Lawrence's viability in the general election are based on an outmoded metric of electability.

Driving the news: Lawrence defeated Bridget Brink, a former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine, and Matt Maasdam, a former Navy SEAL and military aide to President Obama, the Associated Press projected Tuesday night.

  • The outcome is what party leaders in both Michigan and D.C. had feared for weeks — that Maasdam and Brink would split the moderate vote and create an opening for Lawrence to win.
  • The race split the establishment down the middle, with the Democratic Women's Caucus backing Brink while Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) threw her support behind Maasdam.

Zoom out: Lawrence is one of several progressives who have beaten more establishment-aligned candidates in key swing districts this election cycle.

  • Progressive activist and political science professor Randy Villegas beat moderate California State Assemblymember Jasmeet Bains in the race to take on Rep. David Valadao (R-Calif.).
  • In Maine, progressive state Auditor Matt Dunlap won a primary victory over establishment-backed Joe Baldacci in the seat of retiring Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine).
  • The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee backed Bains and Baldacci but did not take a side in Michigan's 7th District.

item.title: U.S. nears Hormuz deal, aiming for Wednesday announcement
item.description:
The U.S., Iran and Oman are closing in on an interim agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with the U.S. aiming for a Wednesday announcement, according to two regional sources and a U.S. official.

Why it matters: The deal, which has been under negotiations for several weeks, is aimed at resuming the ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran and restarting negotiations over a nuclear deal.

  • President Trump decided on Saturday not to follow through on threats to unleash a massive bombing campaign, in order to allow more time for diplomacy. If a deal isn't reached soon, however, Trump could green-light major strikes.
  • The emerging deal would meet some of Iran's demands for greater control over traffic in the Strait of Hormuz — control it didn't have before the war.

Driving the news: According to two regional sources, the deal under discussion sets up a 60-day temporary arrangement between Oman and Iran in the Hormuz strait, which could be extended.

  • All inbound traffic of ships through the strait and into the Gulf would go in a northern lane through Iranian waters.
  • All outbound traffic through the strait and into the Arabian Sea would go in a southern lane through Omani waters, in coordination with Iran.
  • No tolls or fees would be charged during the 60-day period.
  • The parties would work on clearing naval mines from the median lane of the strait within 30 days.
  • After the median lane is cleared, it would be used for inbound and outbound traffic under the terms of a permanent arrangement to be negotiated between Oman and Iran.

Yes, but: The White House, Oman and regional mediators thought they had a deal with Iran three weeks ago, only to see Iran resume attacks on ships. That led to two weeks of fighting and almost an all-out war.

Behind the scenes: In addition to the talks between Oman and Iran, Qatari, Pakistani and Saudi officials were also involved in the mediation efforts, regional sources say.

  • The White House was actively involved in the negotiations, the regional sources said. In recent days, there were several calls between Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi.
  • Two regional sources said Araghchi agreed in principle over the weekend but still needed approval from Iran's Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, and the Supreme National Security Council.
  • A U.S. official and a regional source said Iranian leadership completed its approval process on Tuesday.

item.title: Establishment Democrats notch rare win as Wesley Bell fends off DSA-backed Cori Bush
item.description:
Rep. Wesley Bell (D-Mo.) defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in his primary on Tuesday, thwarting an attempt by left-wing groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America, to avenge Bush's 2024 loss.

Why it matters: It's a win for the Democratic establishment in an election cycle where triumphs against left-wing insurgents have been few and far between.

  • Bell's win was propelled in part by United Democracy Project, the super PAC arm of AIPAC, which spent more than $3 million to thwart Bush's comeback, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
  • Bell was also endorsed by House Democratic leadership and the Congressional Black Caucus, while Bush had the backing of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and left-wing groups such as DSA and the Justice Democrats.

Driving the news: Bell led Bush by 45 percentage points with about a quarter of precincts reporting as of Tuesday evening, with the Associated Press projecting he would win the nomination.

  • Bush, a former progressive organizer, represented the St. Louis-based seat from 2021 to 2025.
  • She lost her 2024 primary to Bell amid a campaign finance scandal and roughly $9 million in AIPAC ad spending.

By the numbers: In addition to UDP, the super PAC of the center-left New Democrat Coalition and the American Bridge-affiliated Project 218 spent another $1.1 million and $250,000, respectively, supporting Bell.

  • Bush was supported by a little over $200,000 in collective outside spending from progressive groups, including MoveOn and the Working Families Party.
  • Bell also out-raised and outspent Bush, bringing in nearly $3.6 million and spending more than $2.9 million as of July 15, compared with Bush's $1.3 million in fundraising and $1.2 million in spending.

What's next: Bell is all but certain to win in November — former Vice President Kamala Harris carried the district by 57 percentage points in 2024.

item.title: Man arrested near Trump golf course after gun found in car
item.description:
Authorities said Tuesday they arrested a suspect near President Trump's Los Angeles-area golf course ahead of his fundraising visit.

The big picture: Jeanine John Taele, 38, of Downey, California, was arrested Sunday after deputies say they found a pistol and illegal ammunition in his vehicle in a parking lot at Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes, according to the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department.

Zoom in: A suspect was "observed walking throughout the golf course grounds taking photographs and videos and appearing to monitor security-planning activities," according to the LACSD statement.

  • Taele was arrested for carrying a concealed firearm and possession of armor-piercing/prohibited ammunition and remains in custody, according to the sheriff's department.
  • "Recognizing the potential security implications surrounding the incident," detectives obtained a search warrant Monday for Taele's home, the LACSD said.
  • They recovered more weapons, ammunition, body armor, two radio signal devices and notebooks "containing concerning statements," according to the statement.

Context: Trump is visiting California this week to attend a Republican National Committee fundraising dinner.

What we're watching: "The investigation is being conducted in close coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Joint Terrorism Task Force and the United States Secret Service," the LACSD said.

Go deeper: Timeline: Shootings, threats against Trump over the years

item.title: Scoop: Inside Hegseth's classified plea for more defense funds
item.description:
Top Pentagon officials are already pitching reconciliation 4.0 to Senate Republicans behind closed doors, underscoring the need for a massive boost in military funds, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Thune hasn't embraced reconciliation 3.0. The White House is already looking beyond it.

  • Trump officials are quietly sketching out a lame-duck package that could pair significant Pentagon funding with other priorities, including a debt ceiling increase that will be necessary sometime in 2027. They see it as going hand in hand with the current effort to pass reconciliation 3.0.
  • The administration's case goes beyond replenishing weapons depleted by the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. Officials are also sounding alarms about the need to invest in artificial intelligence now as China advances.
  • In the shorter term, the White House is pushing the House's version of the budget resolution, which only includes $67 billion in defense spending.

Driving the news: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and several undersecretaries gave Republican members of key Senate committees a detailed, closed-door briefing Tuesday morning, according to two sources familiar with the meeting.

  • The officials gave an around-the-world threat analysis, laying out for senators how the U.S. stacks up against key adversaries — with an emphasis on China, the sources said.
  • Emil Michael, undersecretary for research and engineering, laid out the importance of significant spending on AI to maintain the U.S.' edge over China.
  • Officials showed "candor" on U.S. munitions stockpiles amid the conflict with Iran, and provided "a level of detail that the committees have been seeking," as one source described it.

The meeting was held in a secure setting, with some classified material covered.

The intrigue: Multiple senators urged the officials to expand their outreach beyond Republicans already sold on a massive increase in defense budgets to try to start winning over senators on the fence.

  • Democrats were not invited to the briefing.
  • They also have been excluded from other recent briefings on Iran, another source familiar with the matter told Axios.

item.title: Congressional Black Caucus plays hardball with Jeffries-skeptic DSA Democrats
item.description:
Some members of the Congressional Black Caucus want a condition for incoming Democrats seeking to join their ranks: You have to support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for speaker.

Why it matters: Things could get dicey fast, as several Black Democrats who are all but guaranteed to be elected in November have declined to commit to voting for Jeffries.

  • But Darializa Avila Chevalier wants in: The Afro-Latino nominee in New York's 13th District told Semafor she will seek to join both the CBC and the Hispanic Caucus if elected.
  • Pennsylvania state Rep. Chris Rabb, the nominee for a Philadelphia-based House seat, told Axios he is "definitely planning to join" the CBC.
  • "I absolutely plan on joining the Black Caucus," said Melat Kiros of Colorado — another Black Democrat running in a safely blue district.

All three DSA-aligned candidates have declined to commit to voting for Jeffries as speaker.

  • Kiros previously told Axios she "will not vote for any Democrat for a leadership position if they take corporate PAC money," which would apply to Jeffries.

What we're hearing: Several members of the Black Caucus, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer frank remarks about likely incoming colleagues, said criticism of Democratic leadership could be an issue.

  • One senior CBC member, when asked if Avila Chevalier would be allowed to join, told Axios: "Not if she doesn't support Hakeem along with other issues."
  • Asked if that would apply to all incoming members, the lawmaker replied, "Yes."
  • Avila Chevalier "absolutely will not be welcomed if she doesn't support Hakeem," said a second CBC member. "Under no circumstances would anyone be welcomed with a warm embrace if they are going to undermine the brotha! Just no path."

Between the lines: Loyalty to Democratic leadership isn't a formal criterion for CBC membership, a source familiar with the matter told Axios, but it may be a de facto one.

  • "Support for Hakeem is not a written rule, at least not yet," the source said, but "it would be a challenge to accept someone in the CBC who doesn't support him for speaker."
  • The source added: "The CBC has far-left people, Squad members, DSA members. ... But they are committed to Black people and the Black agenda. Hakeem Jeffries as speaker of the House is about progress for Black people and the Black agenda."
  • "You can't come to the CBC and blow up the point of the CBC. It does not make sense."

Yes, but: The second House Democrat who spoke on the condition of anonymity stressed that while these members may not be welcomed with open arms, it doesn't mean they will be turned away entirely.

  • "We have had Republicans," the lawmaker noted. The CBC allowed former GOP Rep. Mia Love to join, though it has denied other Republicans.
  • The group has also rebuffed some Democrats, including Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.), the Afro-Latino chair of the Hispanic Caucus, whom Avila Chevalier unseated in June.

A Democratic leadership source strongly pushed back against the notion that any incoming Black Democrats would be denied entry to the CBC based on their vote for speaker.

  • "I don't believe the CBC decides its membership based on one's pledge to support leadership," the source said, adding that Avila Chevalier "will get the same review process as everyone else."
  • "I don't think it's a thing at the end of the day," the source said.

The bottom line: "As with every new Congress, matters related to membership for the 120th Congress will be addressed following the 2026 election cycle through the Congressional Black Caucus's established processes," a CBC spokesperson told Axios.

  • "Right now, our focus is on voting rights while remaining committed to advancing policies that expand opportunity, protect fundamental rights, and improve the lives of the communities we serve."
